decision_lens: Does the generation system produce infinite variety from finite, constrained vocabulary? Is the palette (species count) sized so that each element is individually recognizable while combinations create emergent patterns? Does the system distinguish between the fixed motif vocabulary and the infinite arrangement grammar?
distance_rationale: Iznik ceramics is a 16th-century Ottoman decorative tradition that solved the procedural generation problem centuries before computers — producing infinite visual variety from a deliberately constrained palette of 4-5 colors and standardized motifs, with hand-variation ensuring no two tiles were identical. This maps directly to the species count and procgen questions but from a domain of workshop ceramic production entirely outside software, ecology, or game design.
expected_isomorphisms: The Iznik chromatic palette (4-5 colors) maps to species count constraint (8-12 vs 20-30). The fixed motif vocabulary (saz, tulip, carnation) with hand-variation maps to fixed archetypes + procgen variants (Q1 Option D). Tile tessellation rules map to how flora entities compose across adjacent terrain tiles. The Iznik decline (too many colors, lost quality control) maps to the risk of too many species diluting the palette. Workshop-scale production maps to ECS entity density feasibility.
focus: Evaluate the flora design questions through the structural logic of Iznik ceramic tilework — where a deliberately constrained chromatic palette expanded and contracted over centuries, where standardized yet hand-varied tiles tessellate into emergent patterns, and where the tension between fixed vocabulary and infinite arrangement defines the art form.
name: fd-iznik-chromatic-constraint
persona: A scholar of Ottoman Iznik ceramics with deep knowledge of how the Iznik palette evolved: early 15th-century cobalt blue and white only, mid-16th-century addition of turquoise and sage green, the late-16th-century breakthrough of Armenian bole red (tomato red) under Suleiman, and the 17th-century decline as quality control faltered. You understand that the Iznik tradition's power came from palette constraint — four or five colors, rigorously controlled, produced more visual richness than unlimited pigment. You know that each tile was hand-painted (no two identical) yet followed standardized motifs (saz leaves, tulips, carnations, cloud bands) that tessellated predictably. The tradition solved the same problem as procedural generation: how to produce infinite variety from finite vocabulary.
review_areas: Palette sizing and species count (Q1): the Iznik tradition's most productive period used exactly 4-5 colors. Too few (blue and white only) was limiting; too many (European maiolica's unlimited palette) produced visual incoherence. Option A's 8-12 species mirrors the Iznik sweet spot — enough for rich composition, few enough that each is recognizable. But the Iznik lesson is that palette size must be EARNED through mastery of each element before adding the next. Did Armenian bole arrive because they mastered the previous palette. Does the design allow for palette expansion over game time — starting with fewer species and adding as the colony matures?

Fixed vocabulary vs. arrangement grammar (Q1): Iznik tiles use standardized motifs (saz leaf, tulip, carnation, cloud band) that appear across thousands of tiles but are never identical — each is hand-painted within the motif template. Option D (6 fixed archetypes + 2-4 procgen) mirrors this perfectly: fixed motifs (archetypes) with hand-varied instances (procgen). But does the design specify the ARRANGEMENT GRAMMAR — the rules for how species combine on a tile, across a field, through a biome? Iznik panels work because motif placement follows compositional rules (symmetry, flowing stems, border patterns), not because the motifs themselves are interesting.

Quality control and the decline (Q1, Q5): the Iznik tradition's 17th-century decline happened when quality control loosened — too many colors, sloppier painting, loss of the Armenian bole technique. Option B's 20-30 species risks the same decline: too many elements, each less carefully realized, the whole less coherent. Does the design have a quality control mechanism — a way to ensure that each species is 'painted' with enough care (distinct soil preferences, beauty values, visual character) that adding more species doesn't dilute the palette?

Tessellation and terrain architecture (Q3): Iznik tiles are individually crafted but designed to tessellate — the edge of one tile continues seamlessly into the next. Option B (overlay) treats terrain as the tile body and flora as the painted surface — the tile tessellates (terrain handles pathfinding, adjacency) while the decoration varies (flora entities add species detail). This is architecturally sound IF the 'tile body' (terrain) provides consistent edges. Does the terrain system guarantee that adjacent tiles have compatible properties for flora to tessellate across?

Standardization enabling scale (Q5): the Iznik tradition produced thousands of tiles for mosque interiors because the motif vocabulary was standardized enough for workshop production. High entity density (Q5 Option A, ~600 entities) is only feasible if species have standardized, lightweight representations — the ECS equivalent of a tile template. Does the component design for flora entities follow a standardized pattern that makes 600 instances as manageable as 600 tiles from the same motif vocabulary?

severity_examples.condition: Q1 specifies per-species generation (soil preference, beauty, growth rate) but no inter-species tessellation rules for how a forest, meadow, or garden composes multiple species
severity_examples.scenario: Species are generated with individual properties but no arrangement grammar — the system knows what each species looks like but not how species combine into compositional patterns across tiles and biomes

severity_examples.condition: Species count exceeds the threshold where each can be given distinct, memorable properties (visual character, gameplay niche, compositional role) and begins to blur into categorical noise
severity_examples.scenario: Option B's 20-30 species dilutes the palette so that individual species lose recognizability — the Iznik decline pattern where more variety produces less quality

severity_examples.condition: Q1 options all generate the full species set at world generation rather than starting with a core palette and introducing new species as the colony's botanical knowledge grows
severity_examples.scenario: All species are generated at world creation with no palette expansion over time, missing the Iznik lesson that palette growth should track mastery

source_domain: Ottoman Iznik ceramic tilework (15th-17th century Iznik tradition)
success_hints: Species count sits in the Iznik sweet spot where each element is individually recognizable and compositionally productive. The design distinguishes between the species vocabulary (fixed motifs) and the arrangement grammar (how species compose across space). There is a quality control mechanism ensuring each species has enough distinct character to justify its existence. High entity density is enabled by standardized, lightweight component templates. The terrain system provides consistent 'tile edges' that allow flora to tessellate across adjacent tiles.
task_context: Six open design questions for a dynamic flora system in an elven colony sim (Rust ECS, WASM). The system needs procedurally generated species (or fixed species) with growth stages, soil preferences, beauty values, and seasonal states. Entity density could range from ~20 sparse entities to ~600 full-coverage entities on a 40x30 map. The tension between 'every world unique' (procgen) and 'shared vocabulary' (fixed species) is central to Q1. The ECS architecture must handle potentially hundreds of flora components efficiently in WASM.
